newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Crude Outlook - Stronger despite open WAf arb.
newsitem.headline: Asia Crude Outlook - Stronger despite open WAf arb.

text.p: In spite of West African cargoes moving into Asia, the outlook for regional heavy crudes is positive, as an overhang in the prompt June market finally disappeared and more Japanese demand for burning crudes was seen for July, traders said on Monday.
The collapse of Brent prices last week halved the August differential between Brent and Dubai from previous weeks, to around 60 cents per barrel.
This narrow Brent/Dubai spread prompted Asian refiners to boost their demand for West African crudes which are priced against dated Brent.
Over 200,000 barrels per day of crudes from Nigeria, Congo and Angola have been sold to Korea, Taiwan and China.

But since these cargoes are only due to arrive in Asia in the second half of August, refiners and utilities in north Asia will still need to cover their July summer requirements with short haul crudes, providing some support for Asian direct burning grades Minas and Widuri, traders said.
July Widuri barrels were already traded at ICP +10 cents per barrel, a sharp contrast to the last June Minas deals that were done at ICP -20.
Minas and Widuri normally trade at similar levels.
"Most shosha with July supplies are not offering spot barrels as they have committments to utilities" said a western oil trader.
"Some are even looking to buy spot cargoes" he said.
But light Asian crude prices are sliding, as maintenance shutdowns in Mobil and Shell's refineries in Australia lead to high crude stocks, forcing sellers to slash their offers to meet buyers' bids.
A July Cossack cargo was traded at Tapis APPI -$1.10, double the discounts for Cossack cargoes sold in the last few months.

Further pressure on the light crude market is likely to come from an increase in the July allocations of light Belida crude from Indonesia, as a result of the maintenance shutdown of Indonesia's Balikpapan refinery.
Balikpapan refines a substantial volume of light sweet crudes, mainly Belida.
Traders expected Belida allocations to reach 20,000 b/d in July, compared to just 6,000 b/d that was allocated in June.
The prevailing weakness in the Middle East crude market is also likely to continue.
The bulk of Asian demand for July Middle East crudes have been covered, leaving few outlets for the last cargoes of Oman and Abu Dhabi crudes.
Availabilities of Yemeni Masila - which is a competitor crude to Oman in terms of quality, but is priced against Brent - limited the interest for the last Oman barrels.
July barrels of Masila were eagerly snapped up as buyers took advantage of the narrow Brent/Dubai differential.
At least one full Oman cargo and some small parcels are still on offer.
With bids coming from MPM -40, Oman prices which had already fallen continuously from MPM -12 to MPM -30 for July, are poised to weaken further.
--Singapore Newsroom (+65 870 3081)
